passages.t: The woman, the child and the dragon
passages.happening:
John sees a sign in the sky: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (verse 1). “She was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth” (verse 2).

Then a second sign: “a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven royal crowns on his heads” (verse 3). His tail sweeps a third of the stars from the sky and throws them to the earth. “And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth” (verse 4).

“And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne” (verse 5). “And the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her to be nourished for 1,260 days” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The seventh trumpet announced that God's kingdom had come. Now the book steps back to show the deep story behind everything the churches have suffered. The conflict is older than Rome and larger than any persecution. It goes back to the serpent in the garden of Genesis 3, and it runs forward to the end. Many see chapters 12 to 14 as the centre of the book.

John calls the woman and the dragon ‘signs’. The Greek word, sēmeion, is used for visions that point beyond themselves. These are symbols to be understood, not figures in the night sky.

The woman wears the sun, the moon and twelve stars. In Joseph's dream the sun, moon and stars stood for his father, mother and brothers, the family of Israel, and twelve is the number of the tribes. And the prophets pictured Zion as a woman in labour, giving birth to a new people. She is splendid, and she is in agony. God's people bring the Messiah into the world through suffering.

The dragon is red, like the horse that took peace from the earth. His seven heads and ten horns come from the monsters of the Old Testament and from Daniel's fourth beast. His crowns claim a right to rule. And his whole aim, in this chapter, is the child.

The child is Jesus. He ‘will rule all the nations with an iron scepter’, in the words of Psalm 2, the psalm of God's anointed king. The whole earthly life of Jesus is pressed into two moments: birth, and being caught up to God's throne. The dragon waited to devour him, as Herod tried to kill the infant Jesus, and failed. The ascension is the answer to the dragon's threat.

Then the woman flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared in advance, and she is fed there for 1,260 days, the same limited season as in chapter 11. The wilderness is a place of danger, but it is where God fed Israel with manna and fed Elijah by the brook.

People in Asia knew stories like this. Many scholars have noted that it resembles the Greek myth of Leto, pursued while pregnant by the serpent Python, who gave birth to the god Apollo; Apollo later killed the serpent, and Ephesus claimed the birth took place near the city. Some emperors linked themselves with Apollo. If John's hearers caught the echo, the point was sharp: the true child who defeats the dragon is not an emperor but Jesus, and the true dragon stands behind the empire, not against it.
passages.ot:
The crown of stars recalls Joseph's dream: “this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me” (Genesis 37:9).

Zion in labour is the prophets' picture: “Writhe in agony, O Daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor” (Micah 4:10), and “before she was in pain, she delivered a boy” (Isaiah 66:7).

The dragon has deep roots. The psalm praises God who “smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea” and “crushed the heads of Leviathan” (Psalm 74:13-14). Isaiah says God “will slay the dragon of the sea” (Isaiah 27:1). Ezekiel calls Pharaoh a “great monster who lies among his rivers” (Ezekiel 29:3). The ten horns are from Daniel's fourth beast, which “had ten horns” (Daniel 7:7), and the falling stars from Daniel 8:10, where a proud king “cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth”.

The child's rule is Psalm 2: “You will break them with an iron scepter” (Psalm 2:9). And behind the whole chapter stands God's first promise: “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15).
passages.hard:
Who is the woman?

She has been read in three main ways since the early church. Hippolytus of Rome, in the early third century, read her as the church, which keeps bringing Christ into the world. The earliest Greek commentary on Revelation that survives, by Oecumenius in the sixth century, read her as Mary, the mother of the Lord, and that reading shaped Catholic and Orthodox devotion; the Catholic lectionary reads verses 1 to 6 on the feast of the Assumption. Many Protestant and modern commentators read her as the people of the Messiah: Israel, from whom he came, and then the church.

Many interpreters conclude that she is the one people of God, Israel giving birth to the Messiah and continuing as the church, with Mary as the mother in whom that people bore its child. The symbols allow these layers, and readers across traditions have held them together. These notes do not choose.

Some who read Revelation against the events of the 60s link the woman's flight with a story told by Eusebius: before the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, the Christians of the city were warned and moved to Pella, east of the Jordan. Most commentators read the wilderness as a symbol with deeper roots, the place where God feeds his people. These notes do not choose.

What about the third of the stars? Many readers have taken them as angels who fell with Satan, a reading that entered the popular imagination through John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667). The text says only that the stars are thrown to the earth, and its clearest background, Daniel 8:10, is about a persecuting king.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that God's people bring Christ into the world through pain. Ask where your own ‘wilderness’ is, and whether you can see God feeding you there. And ask what powers in your world claim crowns that belong only to Christ.

passages.happening:
The scene moves to heaven: “Then a war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back” (verse 7). “But the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels” (verse 8).

“And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Michael's name means ‘Who is like God?’ In Daniel he is the angelic prince who stands guard over Israel. Here he and his angels fight the dragon, and the dragon loses his place in heaven.

Notice that Michael, not Christ, fights this battle. That fits the chapter. The decisive victory has already been won by the Lamb, as the hymn in verse 11 will say. The angels' war carries out its result.

Then the dragon is named, with a string of titles that gather up the Bible's whole account of evil. He is ‘that ancient serpent’, the serpent of Genesis 3. He is ‘the devil’, a Greek word meaning slanderer. He is ‘Satan’, a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser. And he is ‘the deceiver of the whole world’. His characteristic work, from the garden onward, is to make people believe a lie about God.

Genesis never calls the serpent Satan. The link grew in Jewish thought before the New Testament, Paul assumes it, and Revelation states it outright here. This is the plainest statement in Scripture that the serpent of Eden and the devil are one.

The word ‘hurled’ comes three times. The dragon who threw a third of the stars to the earth (verse 4) is now himself thrown down.
passages.ot:
Michael is Daniel's guardian of God's people: “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up” (Daniel 12:1).

The accuser stands before God in Zechariah's vision: “Then the angel showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, with Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him” (Zechariah 3:1).

And the ancient serpent is the one in the garden, to whom God said, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15).
passages.hard:
When was Satan thrown out of heaven?

Readers answer in more than one way, and these notes do not choose. Some read the war as a rebellion at the very beginning, before the fall of humanity, drawing on passages such as Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 (which in their setting speak of the kings of Babylon and Tyre). Futurists often place it in a final period still to come. Many others read it as the heavenly side of the cross, resurrection and ascension. The hymn that follows says the saints conquered ‘by the blood of the Lamb’, and Jesus linked Satan's fall to his own ministry and death: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18), and “now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31).

These positions are held by faithful readers. The chapter's claim, that the accuser is defeated, stands on each.
passages.asks: Ask what lies about God you have found it easiest to believe. Ask what it means that the deceiver of the whole world has already lost his place. And ask whether you think of evil as stronger than it is, or weaker than it is.

passages.t: Conquered by the blood of the Lamb
passages.happening:
John hears a loud voice in heaven explain what he has seen: “Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ. For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down— he who accuses them day and night before our God” (verse 10).

“They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death” (verse 11).

“Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them! But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This song is the key to the chapter. What looked like a battle of angels is explained as the result of the cross and of faithful witness on earth.

The devil is called ‘the accuser of our brothers’. The Greek word, katēgōr, is a legal word for a prosecutor. His work was to bring charges against God's people before God, day and night. Now he has been thrown down. There is no longer any court where a believer can be condemned, because Christ's death has answered every charge.

‘They have conquered him.’ The word for conquer, nikaō, was used in every one of the seven letters: ‘to the one who overcomes’. Here conquering is given its true meaning. God's people conquer by the Lamb's blood, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives so much that they would deny him to save them.

Then the reason the church still suffers. Heaven rejoices, because the dragon is gone. But the earth is warned, because he has come down there, furious, ‘knowing he has only a short time’. The church does not suffer because Satan is winning. It suffers because he has lost and knows it. That does not make suffering less painful. But it changes what it means.
passages.ot:
The accuser is the one Job's story shows before God, and the one Zechariah saw ‘to accuse’ the high priest (Zechariah 3:1). In Zechariah the LORD rebukes the accuser, takes away the high priest's filthy clothes, and says, “See, I have removed your iniquity” (Zechariah 3:4).

The joining of ‘our God’ and ‘His Christ’ is Psalm 2's ‘the LORD’ and ‘His Anointed One’ (Psalm 2:2).

And the call to the heavens to rejoice is the psalms' call: “Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice” (Psalm 96:11).
passages.hard:
‘They did not love their lives so as to shy away from death.’ Does this mean Christians should seek to die for their faith?

No. The verse honours believers who were faithful when faithfulness cost them their lives. They did not seek death. They refused to deny Christ, and others killed them for it. Their victory was not their death but their faithfulness, and it rested on the Lamb's blood, not on their own suffering. Nothing in this verse asks anyone to put their life in danger, or to harm themselves, to prove their faith. Jesus' own words stand behind it: whoever loses his life for his sake will save it, and he spoke of a life given in faithfulness, never thrown away.

What the verse offers is comfort. The accuser who charged God's people day and night has been thrown down. “Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what accusations you still listen to that Christ's death has already answered. Ask what ‘conquering’ would look like in your life on the Lamb's terms. And ask how it changes your view of hardship to see it as the fury of a defeated enemy.

passages.happening:
Thrown to the earth, the dragon “pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child” (verse 13). “But the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness, where she was nourished for a time, and times, and half a time” (verse 14).

“Then from the mouth of the serpent spewed water like a river to overtake the woman and sweep her away in the torrent” (verse 15). “But the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that had poured from the dragon’s mouth” (verse 16).

“And the dragon was enraged at the woman, and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the dragon stood on the shore of the sea” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The story goes back to verse 6 and explains it. The Greek word for ‘pursued’ can also mean ‘persecuted’, and both fit. The church's experience of persecution is the dragon's pursuit.

But the woman is ‘given’ two wings of a great eagle. At Sinai God told Israel that he had carried them out of Egypt on eagles' wings. The church is carried as Israel was carried. She is not taken out of the wilderness. She is protected in it, and fed there, for ‘a time, and times, and half a time’, Daniel's limited season of trouble, the same as the 1,260 days.

The serpent tries a flood. The earth itself takes her side and swallows the river. At the Red Sea, and in the wilderness, creation fought for God's people. In the end creation will not cooperate with evil.

So the dragon turns on ‘the rest of her children’, believers on earth. They are known by two marks: they keep God's commandments, and they hold to the testimony of Jesus. They are the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15.

And the dragon takes his stand on the shore of the sea. That is where chapter 13 begins: the dragon's agents are about to rise.
passages.ot:
The eagle's wings are God's words at Sinai: “how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself” (Exodus 19:4).

The earth opening its mouth echoes Korah's rebellion, when “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them” (Numbers 16:32), and the song of the sea: “You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them up” (Exodus 15:12).

And the wilderness is where God fed his people: “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35). He fed Elijah there too: “I have commanded the ravens to feed you there” (1 Kings 17:4).
passages.asks: Ask where you have been carried through a time you could not have survived alone. Ask whether others would know you by those two marks: keeping God's commandments, and holding to the testimony of Jesus. And ask how it helps to know that the season of pursuit has a limit.
